title: Devapala and the King from the Sea

title_i18n.en: Devapala and the King from the Sea

subtitle: When Nalanda Spoke to the Sea
region: Bengal, Bihar, Nalanda and Suvarnadvipa in Sumatra
moral: Learning can make distant shores neighbors.

sources.citation: Nalanda Copper Plate of Devapala, regnal year 33; S.K. Mitra, Epigraphia Indica 17, 1923-24
sources.note: Primary record of Balaputradeva's request and the five-village grant.

sources.citation: H.B. Sarkar, Cultural Relations between India and South-East Asian Countries, 1985
sources.note: Classic study of Sailendra-Pala cultural links.

sources.citation: Himanshu Prabha Ray, ed., The Archaeology of Seafaring in Ancient South Asia, Cambridge University Press, 2003
sources.note: Recent maritime context for Bay of Bengal religious and diplomatic networks.

panels.shot: split composition, half showing a regal court in Bengal, half a distant island shore with ships, joined by a glowing copper plate at the center

dialogue.text: In Devapala’s thirty-third year, a king from the sea wrote to Nalanda—binding Bengal to Sumatra with five villages and a single copper plate.

panels.shot: wide aerial over the eastern Indian subcontinent, slow drift from Bengal’s rivers to the Bay of Bengal and beyond

dialogue.text: By the ninth century, Bengal’s rivers did not end at the sea. They flowed into a wide world of winds, ships and islands that Indian texts called Suvarnadvipa—the Island of Gold.

panels.shot: medium close on Devapala’s half of the character sheet, courtly low-angle, with faint overlay of armies and temples behind him

dialogue.text: In this age, Devapala of the Pala line ruled from Bengal and Bihar, famed in inscriptions as a powerful protector of the dharma and patron of monasteries like Nalanda.

panels.shot: medium on Balaputradeva’s half of the character sheet, seated on an island throne with sea beyond, three-quarter profile

dialogue.text: Across the Bay, in Suvarnadvipa, Balaputradeva of the Sailendra house held an island realm, shaped by both local seas and long memories of Indian teachers and texts.

panels.shot: intercut close-ups: Devapala studying a palm-leaf manuscript, Balaputradeva gazing at a bronze Buddha; both lit by lamplight

dialogue.text: Both courts heard of Nalanda, the great monastery in Bihar, where monks from many lands studied logic, grammar and the Buddha’s path under Pala protection.

panels.shot: wide shot of Nalanda’s red-brick complex, slightly elevated, monks moving through corridors

dialogue.text: Nalanda was not just walls of brick. It was a living network of villages and endowments, feeding thousands of monks, copying manuscripts, and drawing students from as far as Southeast Asia.

panels.shot: medium interior of Balaputradeva’s council chamber, angled from the side, focus on a monk pointing at a map

dialogue.text: “Mahārāja, let our island support a house of learning at Nalanda,”

panels.shot: close-up on Balaputradeva’s thoughtful face, slight downward angle, as he makes a decision

dialogue.text: Balaputradeva chose not to send warriors or merchants, but a request. He would honor Nalanda, and seek from Devapala a lasting place for his own foundation there.

panels.shot: dynamic low-angle view from a ship’s deck, crew hauling sails, Balaputradeva’s envoys at the prow

dialogue.text: So the sea carried his message. Envoys from Suvarnadvipa crossed the Bay of Bengal, bearing gifts and a petition from a monarch who called himself ‘king of the island realm.’

panels.shot: wide shot of Devapala’s court in Bengal, with envoys arriving, viewed from behind their shoulders toward the throne

dialogue.text: “O Devapala, guardian of Nalanda, Balaputradeva of Suvarnadvipa sends greetings,”

panels.shot: close on Devapala’s hands unrolling the petition, overhead view of the script lines

dialogue.text: The petition asked that lands be granted near Nalanda, to support a monastery founded by Balaputradeva, in the name of both kings and for the welfare of the sangha.

panels.shot: medium three-quarter shot of Devapala in consultation with monks and ministers, triangle composition

dialogue.text: “This gift will bind Nalanda to the seas, and our name to theirs,”

panels.shot: close-up of an artisan engraving on a sheet of copper, side-light catching the incised letters

dialogue.text: Devapala agreed. In his thirty-third regnal year, a copper plate charter was ordered, naming five villages and confirming the grant for Balaputradeva’s monastery at Nalanda.

panels.shot: wide rural shot of Bengal villages, with farmers in fields and a Nalanda monk arriving, slightly raised viewpoint

dialogue.text: Those five villages—named line by line in the inscription—were woven into Nalanda’s support. Fields, water, and grain in Bengal would now sustain a Sumatran king’s foundation.

panels.shot: interior of a new monastery block at Nalanda, with a discreet Sailendra emblem, monks settling in

dialogue.text: Within Nalanda, a new establishment took shape under Balaputradeva’s name, a Sailendra imprint inside a Pala-guarded university, merging island devotion with Gangetic scholarship.

panels.shot: symbolic split-panel: present-day archaeology overlaid with ghostly image of Devapala and Balaputradeva standing behind the copper plate

dialogue.text: Centuries later, Nalanda’s ruins lay silent. But when the copper plate was found and read, it spoke again of that day when two distant kings shared one monastery in ink and metal.

panels.shot: medium shot of a modern scholar in a library or study, reading a facsimile of the inscription, maps of the Bay of Bengal on the wall

dialogue.text: For historians, this is not a tale of conquest or trade tribute. It is clear, epigraphic proof that Pala Bengal stood inside a Buddhist world reaching across the Bay to the Sailendra islands.

panels.shot: slow push-in on the copper plate itself, displayed against a dark background, letters crisp and highlighted

dialogue.text: On this single sheet of copper, Devapala’s name, Balaputradeva’s title, and five village names fix a moment when learning made Bengal and Sumatra neighbors without a sword being drawn.

panels.shot: final contemplative wide shot: stylized Bay of Bengal at dusk, faint outlines of Nalanda and a Sumatran shrine on opposite horizons, linked by a glowing script line

dialogue.text: The copper plate of Devapala and Balaputradeva reminds us that empires fade, but when a king uses his power to endow learning, even an ocean can become a quiet corridor between minds.
